newsitem.title: USA: House panel joins Senate for US ag research revamp.
newsitem.headline: House panel joins Senate for US ag research revamp.

text.p: Congress was headed Tuesday for the first overhaul of U.S. agricultural research programs in two decades.

The federal government spends about $1.8 billion a year on ag research, which is regarded as the foundation of the thriving farm and food sector. But there are complaints funds are not fairly distributed or squandered on picayune projects.

In launching a series of hearings, House Agriculture subcommittee chairman Larry Combest said he was willing to restructure ag research if it would mean a bigger payoff. Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar took the same stance earlier this year.
"We always seem to assume what we have today is the best," said Combest, Texas Republican. "Just because it's the status quo today, I don't think it necessarily means it should be tomorrow."

The Democratic leader on the subcommittee, Cal Dooley of California, urged innovative thinking to streamline and target research work. Combest said it had been 20 years since a comprehensive ag research bill was considered by Congress.

Lawmakers on the House and Senate agriculture committees were enthused about the idea of setting research priorities thorugh new advisory committees whose membership would include farmers and business representatives.

A discussion paper circulated by the Senate Agriculture Committee suggests that research "must be of multi-state or national relevance" to receive federal funds. Research also would face scientific peer review to assess its soundness.

The National Association of State Universities and Land-Grant Colleges, a major power in ag research, was dubious about creating new advisory boards and said peer review was appropriate in most cases.

Thayne Dutson of Oregeon State University said the land grant colleges believed two other ideas -- requiring 25 percent of research funding to go to mult-state research that was multi-institutional and multidisciplinary and letting any school compete for some types of Extension Service funding -- were burdensome and unwise.
Dutson did not say where the two ideas arose. Both were in the Senate Agriculture Committee's discussion paper.

A spokesman for Lugar, Indiana Republican, said land-grant college support for peer review of research was "important and encouraging." He viewed the colleges as generally in agreement with Lugar's goals and said questions about funding and advisory panels would be tackled in further discussions.
When a research bill is filed, he said, it "will reflect their input. At this point, the bill has not been drafted."

Agriculture Department proposals for ag research should be available for a July 16 hearing by Combest's panel, said Bob Robinson, head of the Cooperative State Research, Education and Extension Service.

Dan Dooley, vice chairman of an Agriculture Department advisory board on research, asked the subcommittee to extend the life of the $100 million a year Fund for Rural America beyond fiscal 1998. The fund supports ag research and rural economic development.
Under the Senate paper, the fund would be extended through 2004 and dedicated to ag research.
